High-level targets you shared:
- P95 latency target: <= 200 ms for short/interactive queries (70% of traffic)
- Throughput target: sustained 120 req/s across peak window
- Concurrency estimate: up to 50 concurrent open requests (burst to 80)
- Streaming requirement: yes — partial token streaming for long responses to improve perceived latency
- Context window: typical input ~8k tokens, some extended documents up to 32k; output usually capped ~2k tokens

Open items we need from Quantix to finalize runbook and sizing:
1) Sample request distributions (attached spreadsheet helps) — token-length histogram and percentiles (p50/p95/p99)
2) Expected qps pattern across your busiest 2-hour window (minute-level if possible)
3) Confirmation on streaming semantics: do you need strict in-order partial outputs, or are chunked paragraphs okay?
4) Security/compliance must-haves for POC (is SOC2 report required to start?)

- Latency/throughput estimates with continuous batching and KV caching enabled; we’ll show expected p95 numbers for the token distributions you provide
- A short-run harness to replay sample payloads and capture p50/p95/p99, plus logs/trace links for each failure mode

- Sales/commercial: draft a short-term reserved capacity recommendation and pricing (Marissa) — target Mon 12/07

Notes on latency tradeoffs (preview):
- With 32k context and 2k output, single-request model compute will be dominated by attention and KV-cache handling; naive full-precision runs typically increase p95 by ~40-70% versus 8k windows
- Continuous batching and prefix KV caching can recover a lot of cost but may add queueing latency that we need to account for in SLOs
- Streaming partial tokens is the fastest UX improvement for long responses while keeping tail latency acceptable

Thanks — attaching the workbook and matrix. If you can send sample payloads I’ll loop Rishi in and we’ll spin up a quick perf harness.

Best,
Sean

Quick technical notes after a cursory look at the sample payloads: thanks Emily for the distribution and minute-level qps. Preliminary observations: 

1) Model selection + context sizing
- With a 32k context and 2k output the compute per request jumps significantly; attention compute scales roughly O(n^2) in sequence length for naive implementations. Our optimized kernels + KV cache help, but the long tails will dominate p95 unless we apply specific mitigations.

2) Suggestion: two-run approach for the POC
- Live tier (interactive): open-model 8k context optimized for p95 <= 200 ms for the 70% short queries. Streaming enabled for medium/long responses.
- Batch/long document tier: quantized 32k-capable model variant routed through a high-throughput lane (higher latency SLO acceptable)

3) Batching and queueing tradeoffs
- Continuous batching with small max-batch (e.g., 8–16) gives best cost/latency tradeoff. Larger batches increase throughput but will add queueing latency that may push p95 above target during bursts.

4) KV cache and prefix reuse
- If a lot of requests reuse common prefixes (templates), enabling prefix caching reduces compute by ~20–35% for those requests; please annotate sample payloads if you have templated prompts.

5) Streaming UX impact
- For long responses, streaming partial paragraphs will reduce perceived latency significantly; it does not eliminate backend compute cost but gives product UX wins while we tune model variants.

Estimated quick numbers (very rough):
- Short query (<=512 tokens) on 8k-cap model with batch size 12: estimated p95 ~ 120–180 ms on our Dedicated GPU profile
- Extended requests (20–32k): p95 can be 800 ms–2.5 s depending on output length and whether quantized model is used

Next steps for Eng:
- We need the minute-level qps CSV and confirmation of templated prompts (Emily)
- I’ll prepare a perf harness and run a 2-hour replay (simulated burst windows) and share p50/p95/p99 traces (target Tue 12/08)

-Rishi
Senior Staff Engineer, Redwood Inference
